newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PGM official sees Japan talks Feb or March.
newsitem.headline: Russian PGM official sees Japan talks Feb or March.

text.p: Russia hopes to hold talks with Japan this month or next on 1997 shipments of platinum group metals (PGM) to Japanese buyers, a top precious metals official said on Tuesday.

Alexander Kulichkov, deputy general director of Almazjuvelirexport, the state precious metals export agency, said, "We're waiting for a government decree (authorising formal talks) and hope that talks will take place this month or next.

"It's unpleasant that we haven't been able to conduct the talks -- but I don't think it has spoiled relations with Japan," Kulichkov said. "We've been working with them for years, and I wouldn't say there's anything catastrophic."

Kulichkov said Russian precious metals producer Norilsk Nickel -- which said on Monday that it would seek to export directly rather than through Almazjuvelirexport -- had not approached him on such a matter.
"They haven't come to us," he said. "But of course, they have the right to turn to the government with this proposal -- they are, after all, the producers.
"But we'll have to wait and see how the government will react. There is, after all, in place an old system (for exporting precious metals through Almazjuvelirexport)."

A Norilsk spokesman said on Monday that the financially-troubled group's new deputy general director, Yuri Kotlyar, a precious metals specialist, would hold talks with the government to allow the group to export its own precious metals to boost revenues instead of going through Almazjuvelirexport.
"We're a state organisation and we pay directly to the budget," Kulichkov said. "If Norilsk were to export, it might pay only taxes, but I don't know -- this is not my sphere of activity."
He said that the issue of who should control Russian exports was not an urgent one for the government, adding, "I think they have a lot of other things to work on as well."
Russia-Japan PGM talks also depend on the federal budget, which the upper parliament house passed last week but which must still be signed into law by President Boris Yeltsin.
